lesson.title: When something goes wrong
lesson.subtitle: Hacked or scammed: tell, take it back, report

video.title: When something goes wrong
video.format_note: Animated explainer for students aged 12–16, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Salma Haddad — maths teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice, talking to the student

scenes.visual: Ms Salma in class; three phones light up with the same message from 'Dina' asking for money, while Dina sits in the front row with her phone switched off.
scenes.animation: Three phones buzz one after another.
scenes.narration: Yesterday, three of my students got the same message from their friend Dina: “Can you send me fifty by mobile money? I’ll pay you back tonight.” But Dina was sitting in my class, with her phone switched off. Someone else had her account.

scenes.visual: Title card with the Darsi mark and the cyber track chip.
scenes.narration: Today: what to do when an account is hacked, or a scam gets you.

scenes.visual: Four warning signs pop around a phone: a sent message the owner never wrote, a password box with a cross, a sign-in alert, a friend asking 'Why do you need money?'.
scenes.narration: How do you know an account was taken? Messages or posts you didn’t send. A password that suddenly doesn’t work. Alerts about a sign-in you didn’t make. Or friends saying you asked them for money.

scenes.visual: A student walks to a parent in the kitchen and shows the phone; the parent nods and sits down beside them.
scenes.animation: Short walk cycle; a heart pops.
scenes.narration: The first step is the hardest, and the most important: tell a trusted adult. Not tomorrow: now. A parent, a guardian or a teacher can help you act fast, and you won’t be in trouble for being tricked.

scenes.visual: A security settings screen: a new password, a two-step switch turning on, a list of devices with 'Sign out', a recovery email with a check.
scenes.animation: Each setting ticks green in turn.
scenes.narration: Then take your account back. Change the password, and anywhere else you used it. Turn on two-step sign-in. Sign out of other devices in the security settings. Check that the recovery email and phone number are still yours.

scenes.visual: Left: a 'Forgot password' button and an official help page. Right: a stranger's chat offering recovery for money, crossed out.
scenes.animation: The stranger's chat gets a red cross.
scenes.narration: Locked out because the thief changed your password? Use the app’s “Forgot password” or its official help page, never someone who offers to recover it for money. Then warn your friends that messages from you weren’t you.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph holds up a phone: a friend's chat says 'Why did you send me this link?'.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A friend says you sent them a strange link last night. You didn’t. What do you do first?

scenes.visual: The 'change and tell' card gets the check badge; a door closes on a shadowy figure.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops; the door shuts.
scenes.narration: Tell a trusted adult and change your password. Someone may be using your account, so close the door before they send more. Then warn your friends not to click.

scenes.visual: A student and a parent call a mobile money helpline from the number on the official card; a screenshot icon saves the chat; a flag and a block sign.
scenes.on_screen_text: Paid or sent a code? Act fast
scenes.narration: Paid a scammer, or sent them a code? Tell an adult straight away, and call the mobile money company or bank on its official number: if you’re quick, money can sometimes be stopped. Keep screenshots as evidence, then report and block.

scenes.visual: Left: a chat 'I can get your money back for a small fee', crossed out. Right: a student with a reassuring hand on the shoulder; a heart.
scenes.narration: Watch out for a second trick: people who promise to get your money back for a fee. That’s another scam. And remember: being tricked isn’t your fault. Scammers are professionals, and they fool adults every day.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph shows a chat: a stranger offers to recover a student's money for a small fee.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Your friend paid for fake game coins and feels stupid. A stranger offers to get the money back for a small fee. What should your friend do?

scenes.visual: Four summary cards: a person telling an adult, a key, a phone call, a flag.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right.
scenes.narration: Say no: that’s a recovery scam. Remember: tell a trusted adult, take your account back, act fast with money, keep evidence and report.

scenes.visual: At the kitchen table, a student and a guardian write a short plan on paper and stick it inside a cupboard door.
scenes.animation: Plan writes itself; end card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it tomorrow: with someone at home, write a short plan on paper: who you’d tell, where the recovery settings are, and the bank or mobile money company’s official number. Keep it somewhere easy to find.

checkpoints.prompt: A friend says you sent them a strange link last night. You didn’t. What do you do first?

options.text: Tell a trusted adult and change my password
Ask more friends if they got it too

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — someone may be using your account. Lock it first, then warn your friends.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — if someone is in your account, every minute lets them send more. Tell an adult and change the password first.

checkpoints.prompt: Your friend paid for fake game coins. A stranger offers to get the money back for a small fee. What should your friend do?

options.text: Say no: tell a parent and report it

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — that’s a recovery scam. Real help, from the bank, the mobile money company or the police, never charges a fee.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — people who charge to recover money are scammers too. Tell a parent, and contact the payment company on its official number.
